brief.title: Contracts — Outline
brief.subject: Concept-first outline for a first-semester contracts course

sections.t: Zehmer, drinking with Lucy, wrote and signed an agreement to sell his farm for $50,000, later claiming it was a joke.
Outward expressions control over secret intent; the contract was enforceable.
Mutual assent is judged objectively, by what a reasonable person would understand.
The company advertised a £100 reward and deposited £1,000 to show sincerity; Mrs. Carlill used the ball and caught flu.
The advertisement was an offer to the world, accepted by performance of the conditions.
A nephew's forbearance from drinking and smoking was consideration for his uncle's promise.
Legal detriment to the promisee suffices; benefit to the promisor is not required.
A promise to provide a home, unsupported by bargain, was a mere gratuity.
A granddaughter who quit work in reliance on a promissory note could enforce it despite the absence of consideration.
Retirement in reliance on a promised pension made the promise enforceable.
A mid-voyage demand for higher pay to do work already owed was unenforceable.
A duty of reasonable efforts was implied, saving the agreement from being illusory.
A cross-collateral clause in an adhesion contract could be unconscionable; remanded for findings.
Unconscionability requires an absence of meaningful choice together with unreasonably favourable terms.
Destruction of the music hall without fault excused both parties.
Damages were the difference between the promised perfect hand and the hand actually given.
Lost mill profits were not recoverable because the carrier was never told of the special circumstances.
Recoverable losses are those arising naturally or in the contemplation of both parties at formation.

brief.overview_html:
This outline is organised by concept, not by case. Each unit opens with a hub concept — Formation, Consideration, Defenses, Terms & Performance, Remedies — with the concepts it contains radiating out from it.

Cases hang off the concepts they support, as chips on the cards. Use the coverage filter to find the concepts your notes are thinnest on.

nodes.title: Formation
nodes.desc: A contract forms on mutual assent to a bargain, supported by consideration.

sections.t: Offer + acceptance + consideration, judged by outward expression rather than secret intent.

nodes.title: Definiteness
nodes.desc: An agreement too indefinite in its material terms is unenforceable even where both sides intended to be bound.

sections.t: Essential terms — parties, subject matter, price, quantity, time — must be reasonably certain.

nodes.title: Preliminary Negotiations
nodes.desc: Invitations to deal, price quotes and most advertisements are not offers.

nodes.title: Offer
nodes.desc: A manifestation of willingness to enter a bargain, so made as to justify another in understanding that assent will conclude it.

sections.t: The offeree must reasonably believe that their assent alone closes the deal.

nodes.title: Revocation
nodes.desc: An offer is freely revocable until accepted, effective on receipt by the offeree.

sections.t: Revocation is effective when received; indirect reliable information of revocation also terminates the power of acceptance.

nodes.title: Option Contracts
nodes.desc: Consideration paid to hold an offer open makes it irrevocable for the stated period.

nodes.title: Unilateral Offers
nodes.desc: An offer inviting acceptance only by performance; part performance makes it irrevocable.

sections.t: An advertisement promising a reward on stated conditions is an offer to the world, accepted by performing them.

nodes.title: Acceptance
nodes.desc: A manifestation of assent to the terms of the offer, made in a manner the offer invites.

nodes.title: Mirror Image Rule
nodes.desc: At common law a purported acceptance varying the offer's terms is a counter-offer, not an acceptance.

nodes.title: Mailbox Rule
nodes.desc: Acceptance is effective on dispatch; revocation, rejection and counter-offers are effective on receipt.

sections.t: Dispatch closes the contract, so an acceptance mailed before a revocation arrives still binds.

nodes.title: Acceptance by Conduct
nodes.desc: Assent may be shown by performance or by conduct recognising the existence of a contract.

nodes.title: Consideration
nodes.desc: A bargained-for exchange: each side's promise or performance induces the other's.

sections.t: A promise is enforceable where the promisee incurs a legal detriment sought by the promisor in exchange.

nodes.title: Bargained-For Exchange
nodes.desc: Detriment to the promisee suffices; forbearance from a legal right is consideration.

sections.t: Giving up a legal right at the promisor's request is consideration, even with no economic benefit to the promisor.
Contrast Hamer, where forbearance was bargained for, with Kirksey, where the promise was a bare gratuity. The pivot is inducement, not value.

nodes.title: Adequacy
nodes.desc: Courts police the existence of a bargain, not the fairness of its terms.

nodes.title: Pre-Existing Duty Rule
nodes.desc: Performing what one is already bound to do is not consideration for a new promise.

sections.t: A modification unsupported by fresh consideration is unenforceable at common law.

nodes.title: Illusory Promises
nodes.desc: A promise reserving unlimited freedom not to perform is no promise at all.

sections.t: A duty of best efforts may be implied to save an otherwise illusory exclusive-dealing agreement.

nodes.title: Reliance Substitutes
nodes.desc: Where a bargain is missing, detrimental reliance may still make a promise enforceable.

nodes.title: Promissory Estoppel
nodes.desc: A promise reasonably expected to induce reliance, and which does induce it, binds if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement.

sections.t: Promise + foreseeable reliance + actual reliance + injustice absent enforcement.

nodes.title: Charitable Subscriptions & Pensions
nodes.desc: Reliance on a gratuitous pension or pledge can supply the missing bargain.

sections.t: An employee who retired in reliance on a pension promise could enforce it though she gave no consideration.

nodes.title: Defenses
nodes.desc: Grounds on which an otherwise-formed contract is void, voidable or unenforceable.

nodes.title: Capacity
nodes.desc: Infants and the mentally incompetent may avoid their contracts.

nodes.title: Duress & Undue Influence
nodes.desc: Assent induced by an improper threat leaving no reasonable alternative is voidable.

nodes.title: Misrepresentation
nodes.desc: A fraudulent or material misstatement inducing justifiable reliance makes the contract voidable.

nodes.title: Unconscionability
nodes.desc: A bargain oppressive in substance and secured by unfair process may be refused enforcement.

sections.t: Requires both procedural unfairness in bargaining and substantive unfairness in terms.

nodes.title: Statute of Frauds
nodes.desc: Certain contracts are unenforceable without a signed writing.

nodes.title: Contracts Within the Statute
nodes.desc: Suretyship, marriage, land, one-year and goods over $500 contracts fall within it.

nodes.title: Satisfying the Writing
nodes.desc: A memorandum signed by the party to be charged, stating the essential terms, suffices.

nodes.title: Terms & Performance
nodes.desc: What the contract means, when performance is due, and what excuses it.

nodes.title: Parol Evidence Rule
nodes.desc: A fully integrated writing bars prior or contemporaneous agreements that contradict it.

sections.t: Total integration bars contradictory and supplementary terms; partial integration bars only contradictory ones.

nodes.title: Interpretation
nodes.desc: Ambiguity is resolved by context, course of dealing, usage of trade and course of performance.

nodes.title: Conditions
nodes.desc: An event that must occur before performance becomes due; non-occurrence discharges the duty.

nodes.title: Material Breach
nodes.desc: A material failure suspends the other side's duty; a minor breach sounds only in damages.

nodes.title: Excuse
nodes.desc: Supervening events may discharge a duty that has become radically different from the one undertaken.

nodes.title: Impracticability
nodes.desc: Performance is excused where an unforeseen event destroys a basic assumption of the contract.

sections.t: Destruction of the subject matter without fault excuses both parties.

nodes.title: Frustration of Purpose
nodes.desc: Performance remains possible but the event has destroyed its whole point.

nodes.title: Remedies
nodes.desc: Expectation is the default; reliance and restitution are the alternatives.

sections.t: Put the injured party where performance would have — not better.

nodes.title: Expectation Damages
nodes.desc: The value of the promised performance less what was saved by not performing.

sections.t: Damages are the difference between the promised result and the result actually obtained.

nodes.title: Reliance Damages
nodes.desc: Out-of-pocket losses incurred in reliance, where expectation cannot be proved.

nodes.title: Restitution
nodes.desc: Recovery of a benefit conferred, measured to prevent unjust enrichment.

nodes.title: Specific Performance
nodes.desc: Available where damages are inadequate — classically for land and unique goods.

nodes.title: Limits on Damages
nodes.desc: Three filters cut expectation down: foreseeability, certainty and mitigation.

nodes.title: Foreseeability
nodes.desc: Damages are limited to losses arising naturally or within the contemplation of both parties at formation.

sections.t: Special losses are recoverable only if the special circumstances were communicated at the time of contracting.
Hadley caps what is recoverable at all; certainty and mitigation then cut the survivors down.

nodes.title: Certainty
nodes.desc: Damages must be proved with reasonable certainty; speculative lost profits fail.

nodes.title: Mitigation
nodes.desc: No recovery for losses the injured party could have avoided by reasonable effort.
